analysis.one_liner: Diverts up to 8 percent of Social Security payroll taxes into individual stock-and-bond accounts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: introduced with only three Republican cosponsors in September 2003, it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee and its Social Security subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would automatically enroll every worker born after 1950 in an individual account funded by a portion of their payroll taxes — up to 8 percent for low earners, less for high earners — invested mostly in stock index funds alongside government bonds. At retirement, the traditional Social Security check would be reduced by roughly the value of what the account pays out, with a guaranteed minimum annuity floor. The transition would be financed from the general federal budget, and the bill directs a study on eventually turning account management over to private firms.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers born after 1950 would own an account that is personal property, invested largely in broad stock indexes, that could pay more than traditional Social Security if markets do well, can be left to heirs, and cannot be changed by a future Congress the way promised benefits can. Low-income workers would get the largest share of their payroll taxes diverted, and a guaranteed minimum annuity (starting near $8,950 a year for a single person, indexed to inflation) would set a floor. Widows and widowers could inherit account balances outright.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an individual account for every worker born on or after January 1, 1950, funded by a share of payroll taxes — 8 percent of wages up to the taxable maximum for low earners, scaling down to 3 percent for the highest earners.

Account balances are invested 65 percent in a broad stock index portfolio and 35 percent in government obligations by default, and are treated as the personal property of the account owner, payable to a surviving spouse or estate on death.

Guarantees a lifetime, inflation-indexed annuity floor at retirement — at least $8,950 a year for a single account owner or $12,120 where dependents qualify, in 2005 dollars — with any balance above that available as cash or additional annuity.

Maintains current payroll tax rates, keeps benefits unchanged for current retirees and near-retirees, and appropriates general-fund money to keep the Social Security trust funds fully funded during the transition.

The fund is run by a federal board modeled on the Thrift Savings Plan, with fiduciary rules, independent annual audits, and a ban on exercising corporate voting rights, designed to keep administrative costs low.

analysis.who_pays: The general federal budget would finance the transition while payroll taxes are diverted into accounts — meaning federal borrowing, other spending cuts, or future taxes. Workers would bear investment risk: their traditional benefit is reduced by roughly the amount the account pays out, choosing riskier portfolios is explicitly at their own risk with no government guarantee, and a worker whose account performs poorly could end up with less than today's promised benefit.
analysis.who_pays_short: General budget; workers bear market risk

drawbacks.text: Traditional Social Security benefits are reduced by an offset equal to what the account would have paid under the default portfolio, so the account does not add to the benefit — it substitutes for part of it, and the worker carries the risk that markets underperform.

The bill states plainly that electing the small- or mid-cap options or changing the stock-bond mix is made at the individual's own risk, with no protection against loss and no government guarantee of return.

The transition is financed from the general budget, which per the bill's own findings would require the government to cover payroll-tax money diverted to accounts — a cost borne by taxpayers generally through borrowing or future taxes.

Enrollment is automatic: every eligible worker is in the program unless they affirmatively opt out within 540 days, and money withdrawn from a closed account reverts to the trust fund rather than back to the worker.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real gains — ownership, inheritability, and a shot at higher returns, with a guaranteed annuity floor protecting the poorest retirees — but the guarantee is narrower than it looks: the annuity floor replaces, rather than adds to, the traditional benefit, and everything above it depends on market performance the bill explicitly does not insure. Meanwhile the transition cost falls on the general budget. Whether workers came out ahead would have depended heavily on when they retired relative to market cycles; the bill would have traded a defined benefit for a largely defined-contribution one.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, then to its Social Security subcommittee, and no one scheduled it for a hearing or a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jim DeMint introduced the Social Security Savings Act of 2003 on September 25, 2003, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Two weeks later, on October 8, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security, where it remained with no further action recorded.
The bill attracted only three cosponsors, all Republicans, and the House never considered it; it died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Traditional Social Security survived intact — current retirees and workers who count on the guaranteed benefit kept the existing system rather than trading a defined monthly check for a market-dependent account. The asset-management industry did not gain the new account business the bill's private-management study envisioned.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Supporters of traditional guaranteed Social Security

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure, but all four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee was the body that let the bill die — private Social Security accounts divided the majority party as much as the minority.

industries.note: The default design keeps the money inside a federally run fund invested by index replication, excluding private managers initially — but the bill orders a study on turning account management over to 'approved account managers' in the private sector once balances grow, a potential multi-hundred-billion-dollar future revenue stream. Workers would own the accounts, but the industry stands to collect fees on managing them.

The bill directs the Executive Director to survey private-sector annuity contracts and to shift to purchasing them whenever their returns are competitive with the government fund — potentially routing retirement payouts through private insurers.

Diverting payroll taxes to accounts while paying full benefits would require new general-fund borrowing, including the special 'Social Security Transition Bonds' the bill creates for the accounts' bond portion.
